questions.q: What is benchmark contamination, and why does it undermine a high benchmark score?
options: Contamination occurs when benchmark test data, or close paraphrases of it, end up in the model's pretraining corpus, so a high score may reflect memorization of the test rather than the capability it was designed to measure
Contamination refers to corrupted files in the benchmark dataset that make it unusable
Contamination only applies to benchmarks that have never been published publicly
Contamination means the benchmark was written by a biased research team
questions.explain: Benchmark contamination means the model may have seen the test questions (or close paraphrases) during pretraining, so strong performance on them doesn't reliably demonstrate the general capability the benchmark intends to measure.

questions.q: Why is contamination described as a near-inevitable risk for models trained on web-scale pretraining data?
options: Because popular benchmarks are public, and a pipeline scraping a large fraction of the public web will likely ingest benchmark-related material unless something specifically filters it out
Because contamination is only a risk for models trained on fewer than 1 million tokens
Because benchmarks are always kept secret and never appear on the public web
Because contamination never actually occurs in modern training pipelines
questions.explain: Since benchmark questions and discussions of them appear across the public web (papers, blogs, GitHub), broad web-scale scraping is likely to capture some of this material unless a deliberate filtering step removes it.

questions.q: What is a limitation of n-gram overlap detection as a contamination-detection method?
options: It requires no tokenization of the benchmark text at all
It always produces false positives on every benchmark example
It catches verbatim or near-verbatim copies but misses paraphrased contamination, where a benchmark question is rewritten in different words while still leaking the same information
It can only be run on models larger than 100 billion parameters
questions.explain: N-gram overlap detection relies on exact matching sequences of tokens, so it reliably catches verbatim copies but can miss contamination where the benchmark content has been paraphrased into different wording.

questions.q: What is a canary string, and what is its key limitation as a defense against contamination?
options: A canary string is a type of GPU hardware sensor used to detect overheating
A canary string guarantees zero contamination with no further action required
A canary string automatically deletes benchmark data from any pretraining corpus it is added to

A canary string is a unique identifier embedded in benchmark data requesting exclusion from pretraining corpora, but it only works if pretraining pipelines actually implement the corresponding filter -- it's an honor-system defense, not an enforced guarantee
questions.explain: A canary string (used by benchmarks like BIG-bench) relies on pretraining pipelines voluntarily checking for and excluding it -- it provides no technical enforcement, making it a voluntary rather than guaranteed defense.

questions.q: How does decontamination as a pretraining pipeline step relate to the deduplication work covered in this course's data curation lessons?
options: Deduplication can only be performed after a model has already finished pretraining
They are entirely unrelated processes with no conceptual overlap
Decontamination is structurally a specific case of unwanted overlap between two datasets, the same category of problem deduplication solves within a single dataset
Decontamination replaces the need for deduplication entirely
questions.explain: Decontamination applies the same overlap-detection logic as deduplication, but checks a pretraining corpus against known benchmark test sets (overlap across datasets) rather than removing duplicates within a single dataset.
